title: LEADERSHIP: Empathy vs. Sympathy Expanded
author: Kyle Shepard
summary: Kyle Shepard uses APA definitions to sharpen the empathy-sympathy distinction: empathy is understanding a person from their own frame of reference (curiosity, requiring removal of one's own biases); sympathy is feeling concern from one's own observation of another's suffering (action-driver). Empathy leads to questions; sympathy leads to action. Chronic sympathy, like chronic stress, produces compassion fatigue, emotional exhaustion, and burnout -- particularly in caregivers, leaders, and coaches. Empathy endures as a sustainable skill. Shepard also introduces 'toxic empathy' -- over-absorption of others' perceived emotions to the point of losing one's own perspective and agency. He concludes both tools are necessary: sympathy starts caring, empathy sustains it productively. The practical summary: consistent curiosity kills chronic concern. Caring has limits, and recognising where sympathy ends and empathy begins enables more effective, longer-lasting service to others.
points: APA definition: empathy = understanding from their frame of reference (curiosity); sympathy = concern from your observation (action-driver).
Chronic sympathy activates the stress response -- sustained concern leads to compassion fatigue, distancing, sleep disruption, and burnout.
Empathy endures as a skill; sympathy wears on the mind and body when applied chronically without recovery.
Toxic empathy: over-empathising causes you to lose your own perspective, intuition, and agency.
Practical rule: 'Consistent curiosity kills chronic concern' -- channel energy into understanding rather than absorbing.
quotes: Empathy is getting out of your own head. It requires removing all of your own biases, opinions, assumptions, and even experiences so you can consider the perspective of the other person. Sympathy is getting another person's head into yours.
Empathy is curiosity whereas sympathy is concern. Empathy leads to questions while sympathy leads to action.

Compassion fatigue, emotional exhaustion, distancing, sleep disturbances, unproductive attitude, and decreased performance are all signs of burnout resulting from mismanaged and/or unrecovered stress. This is an issue in overly sympathetic people and providers.

I often argue the most important attribute one can possess is giving a shit. If you don't care, you won't act. The second most important attribute, however, is not giving too much of a shit. Caring has limits.
